text: {"answer": "Nuclear power has real strengths as a low-carbon option. Its lifecycle emissions per unit of electricity are comparable to wind and lower than solar, making it one of the lowest-carbon sources available [nuclear#0]. Its firm, weather-independent output could reduce the storage a decarbonised grid would otherwise need [nuclear#1], and countries with large existing nuclear fleets decarbonised their grids faster than comparable countries relying on renewables alone [nuclear#2]. Its land use per unit of energy is also far lower than wind or solar [nuclear#3]. The contradicting evidence is substantial, however. Construction timelines of a decade or more mean new reactors may not cut emissions within near-term climate windows [nuclear#5]. Recent European and North American projects ran years late and well over budget, making costs uncompetitive with renewables [nuclear#4], and cost overruns have pushed several utilities into severe distress [nuclear#7]. Waste disposal also remains unresolved, as no country has commissioned a permanent high-level waste repository at scale [nuclear#6].
